title: Written asthma action plan completeness at discharge and 90-day emergency revisits in children
subtitle: Cohort of 2022 to 2025 discharges linked to provincial emergency visits
statement: Children admitted with asthma are meant to leave with a complete five-section written action plan, but a local review found 41 of 90 plans missing at least one section. It is not known whether a complete plan at discharge is associated with fewer asthma emergency revisits or readmissions within 90 days once severity, previous admissions and family circumstances are taken into account. The answer decides whether an electronic plan with forced fields is worth funding.
whoAffected: Children aged 2 to 17 admitted with asthma (about 620 a year), their parents and caregivers, the respiratory educators and ward nurses who write the plans, and the community hospitals that see revisits the children's hospital never learns about.
whatHurts: An emergency revisit means another night of breathlessness, missed school and work, and sometimes a readmission. Incomplete plans leave families without clear steps for the yellow zone or a booked follow-up, and families with limited English may be least able to fill the gaps themselves.
currentPractice: A five-section paper plan is written at discharge by the ward nurse or respiratory educator and scanned into the chart. Completeness is not measured routinely, and revisits to other hospitals are invisible to the discharging team.
whyNow: A proposal for an electronic plan with forced fields is waiting for funding, the winter review showed frequent missing sections, and ethics approval for secondary use of charts has just been granted.
patientCenteredGoal: Every child goes home with a plan the family can use, and fewer children need emergency care for asthma in the three months after discharge.
summary: Problem framed as a cohort question: is a complete action plan at discharge associated with fewer 90-day asthma emergency revisits after accounting for severity and family circumstances?
